planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; var. sinensis is the small-leaved, cold-hardy China botanical variety of the tea plant, distinct from the tropical broad-leaved var. assamica.

directions: Var. sinensis is the small-leaved, shrubby, cold-hardy botanical variety of the tea plant, native to the mountains of southwestern China, and is the parent stock behind most of the world's named green, white, and oolong tea cultivars. Its narrow, finely serrated leaves and slow, dense branching habit make it far more tolerant of winter cold than the tropical var. assamica, and it is the type most reliably grown outside the humid subtropics. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil required by all tea camellias, with morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter climates. Named regional selections of this variety span from Japanese sencha cultivars to Chinese oolong mother trees.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; TV1 is a tropical Assam-type clone best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: TV1 was released in 1949 by the Tocklai Tea Research Institute in Assam, India, as the first vegetatively propagated commercial tea clone, and it remains one of the most widely planted clones in Assam's tea belt, prized for producing a consistent, high-quality CTC (crush-tear-curl) black tea. It is a broad-leaved, vigorous Assam-type selection and shows moderate tolerance of common tea pests and diseases relative to older seedling plantings. In cultivation it wants warm, humid conditions, acidic well-drained soil, and regular pruning to maintain a low plucking table. Its long commercial track record makes it a useful reference clone for comparing yield and cup quality against other named tea selections.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kanayamidori is a Japanese registered cultivar (Norin registration) suited to USDA zones 7-9.

directions: Kanayamidori is a registered Japanese green tea cultivar, selected from Yabukita lineage in Shizuoka and noted for an unusually rich, milky, creamy character in the finished sencha, tied to its elevated concentration of methylated catechins compared with the standard Yabukita cultivar. It grows as a dense, small-leaved China-type shrub and is processed the same way as other Japanese sencha cultivars, steamed shortly after picking to halt oxidation and preserve its bright green color. Give it the standard acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and partial shade tea camellias prefer, with protection from harsh afternoon sun in hot climates. It is grown as a specialty companion cultivar alongside Yabukita in several Japanese tea-producing regions.
sources: Japan Tea Central Public Interest Incorporated Association

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Saemidori is an early-ripening Japanese cultivar suited to USDA zones 7-9.

directions: Saemidori was bred at Japan's Makurazaki research station in Kagoshima by crossing the dominant Yabukita cultivar with Asatsuyu, registered in 1990 as Tea Norin No. 40. It buds out earlier in spring than Yabukita and is especially prized for shaded-culture teas such as gyokuro and tencha (matcha base leaf), where its naturally sweet, low-astringency character and vivid green color are considered top-tier. The shrub carries small, glossy dark leaves on a compact, upright frame. Cultivate it exactly as other Japanese sencha-type cultivars, with acidic, well-drained soil, consistent moisture, and shade cloth or overhead shading in the weeks before harvest if grown for gyokuro-style leaf.
sources: Makurazaki Tea Research Station, Kagoshima, Japan
Japan Tea Central Public Interest Incorporated Association

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Sayamakaori is a cold-tolerant, early-ripening Japanese cultivar suited to USDA zones 6-9.

directions: Sayamakaori is a registered early-ripening Japanese green tea cultivar selected in 1958 at Saitama Prefecture's tea experimental station, developed for the cooler, more northerly Sayama tea-growing region where it is especially prized for its pronounced, distinctive aroma. Its comparatively good cold tolerance for a China-type cultivar makes it a useful choice outside Japan's warmest tea belts. The shrub produces small, narrow leaves typical of fine sencha cultivars and buds early in spring, giving growers a head start on the first flush. Cultivate with the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and partial shade other China-type tea selections require.
sources: Japan Tea Central Public Interest Incorporated Association

common_name: Mi Lan Xiang Tea (Honey Orchid Dan Cong)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Mi Lan Xiang is a Phoenix Mountain oolong cultivar suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Mi Lan Xiang, literally 'honey orchid fragrance,' is the single most widely planted of the named Phoenix (Feng Huang) Dan Cong cultivars from the Chaozhou highlands of Guangdong, China, chosen for oolong processing that brings out sweet, nectarine-like fruit and orchid aromatics with a lingering honeyed finish. It grows as a large-leaved, upright arbor-type shrub, distinct from the small compact China-type bushes used for most green teas, and traditionally develops into a substantial small tree if left unpruned at high elevation. Processing follows classic oolong methods, withering, bruising, partial oxidation, and roasting, to develop its signature aroma, so home growers wanting the characteristic flavor should replicate oolong rather than green-tea processing. Give it warm, humid conditions and the same acidic, well-drained soil required by other tea camellias.

common_name: Ya Shi Xiang Tea (Duck Shit Aroma Dan Cong)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Ya Shi Xiang is a Phoenix Mountain oolong cultivar suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Ya Shi Xiang is a named Phoenix (Feng Huang) Dan Cong cultivar from Ping Keng Tou village in the Guangdong highlands, whose deliberately unappealing name, Chinese for 'duck droppings aroma,' was reportedly chosen by the farmer who first propagated it to discourage others from taking cuttings, despite the tea itself having a delicate, floral, honeysuckle-and-almond character. Like other Dan Cong selections it is a large-leaved arbor type suited to warm, humid highland conditions and traditional oolong processing, withering, bruising, partial oxidation, and roasting, rather than green tea methods. It is considered one of the most important and widely grown of the classic Dan Cong aroma cultivars. Cultivate with the acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil standard to all tea camellias.

common_name: Song Zhong Tea (Song Dynasty Dan Cong)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Song Zhong is a Phoenix Mountain oolong cultivar suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Song Zhong ('Song cultivar') traces its name to old tea trees on Guangdong's Wudong Mountain believed to descend from stock identified during the Song Dynasty roughly 900 years ago, making it one of the most storied of the Phoenix Dan Cong cultivars, an F1 relative of Shui Xian. It is a large-leaved arbor-type tea tree that, left unpruned in its native high-elevation habitat, can grow into a substantial small tree over centuries; garden plants stay far more manageable with regular pruning. The cup carries a classic orchid character with subtle stone-fruit and light spice notes when processed as oolong through the standard withering, bruising, oxidation, and roasting steps. Provide the acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and warm, humid conditions common to all tea camellias.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in zone 9; CA 538 INTA is best established from grafted or vegetatively propagated stock rather than seed.

directions: CA 538 INTA is a commercial yerba mate cultivar developed over decades of breeding by Argentina's INTA research station at Cerro Azul, Misiones, and registered with Argentina's national seed registry (INASE) in 2016. It has become a standard high-yield reference cultivar across the Paraguay-Argentina-Brazil mate-growing region, valued for medium-sized leaves, abundant and uniform new-growth flushes, and strong vigor compared with unselected seedling plantings. In gardens it grows and is harvested the same way as species yerba mate, a large, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub or small tree yielding leaf for the traditional roasted, grassy infusion, but with more consistent, heavier production. Give it moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and partial shade to protect against summer leaf scorch.
sources: INTA (Instituto Nacional de Tecnologia Agropecuaria), EEA Cerro Azul, Misiones, Argentina
INASE (Instituto Nacional de Semillas, Argentina) cultivar registry
